alt: A de jure right exists in law, as when US law gave Black men the vote in 1870; a de facto right exists in practice, and for decades many could not use that vote in the South. Protests often target the gap between the two. Below, rights split into civil and political, and economic, social and cultural.
caption: A right on paper is not always a right in practice; protests often target the gap.

after: ## The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)
alt: The non-binding UDHR of 10 December 1948 leads to two binding 1966 treaties, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, in force from 1976 for ratifying states. Together they form the International Bill of Human Rights.
caption: The UDHR is a declaration; the 1966 covenants are the binding treaties.

after: ## The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)
alt: Four apartheid measures linked to the UDHR articles they breached: racial classification under the Population Registration Act breached Article 2; the Group Areas Act and pass laws breached Article 13 on freedom of movement; denying the Black majority the vote breached Article 21.
caption: Name the law, say what it did, then match it to an article.

alt: Three timelines side by side. US civil rights: Brown v. Board 1954, the Montgomery Bus Boycott 1955 to 1956, Greensboro 1960, Birmingham and the March on Washington 1963, the Civil Rights Act 1964 and the Voting Rights Act 1965. Anti-apartheid: the Defiance Campaign 1952 to the first all-race election in 1994. British women’s suffrage: NUWSS 1897 to equal franchise in 1928.
caption: Accurate, dated evidence from each movement is what examiners reward.

alt: Seven categories of protest from persuasion through legal action, non-cooperation and non-violent intervention to militant action against property and armed struggle, plus international pressure, each with an example such as the March on Washington, the Montgomery Bus Boycott or Umkhonto we Sizwe. Three are marked as Gene Sharp’s headings of non-violent action.
caption: Classify a method before explaining why a movement chose it.

alt: Four questions applied to the Montgomery Bus Boycott: its aim, ending segregated bus seating, was achieved in law in 1956; in practice schools and voting stayed segregated for years; it was a short-term local win that made King a national figure; it worked through economic pressure, unity for 381 days and a parallel court case.
caption: Measure success against the movement’s own aims, in law and in practice, short and long term.

alt: Bars for fictional Norland: the registered share of 480,000 eligible minority adults rose from 25% (120,000) to 65% (312,000) five years after a voting rights law. That is a rise of 40 percentage points, while the number registered rose by 160%.
caption: A rate rising from 25% to 65% is 40 percentage points; registering is not the same as voting.
